court: Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit

issues.label: Subject-matter jurisdiction
issues.why: The court must confirm federal-question jurisdiction over §1983 constitutional claims.

issues.label: Personal jurisdiction
issues.why: The court must ensure it has jurisdiction over each defendant based on contacts with the forum.

issues.label: Venue propriety
issues.why: The court must confirm venue is proper in the Eastern District of Virginia for the events and defendants.

issues.label: Sovereign immunity Virginia
issues.why: The Commonwealth of Virginia is generally immune from suit in federal court under the Eleventh Amendment absent waiver or abrogation.

issues.label: State as §1983 defendant
issues.why: A State is not a “person” under §1983, barring damages and typically barring §1983 claims against it.

issues.label: Official-capacity immunity
issues.why: Claims for damages against state officials in their official capacities are barred by the Eleventh Amendment.

issues.label: Ex parte Young exception
issues.why: The court must determine whether prospective injunctive relief may proceed against proper state officials notwithstanding immunity.

issues.label: Proper defendant for injunction
issues.why: Injunctive relief requires defendants with authority to implement the requested relief at the relevant facility/system.

issues.label: Mootness of injunction request
issues.why: Carter’s transfer/release from Sussex may moot facility-specific injunctive claims unless an exception applies.

issues.label: Mootness exceptions
issues.why: The court must assess voluntary cessation, capable-of-repetition-yet-evading-review, or statewide-policy exceptions.

issues.label: Standing for each remedy
issues.why: Carter must show ongoing or imminent injury for injunctive relief and traceability/redressability for each claim.

issues.label: PLRA exhaustion is mandatory
issues.why: The court must apply 42 U.S.C. §1997e(a) requiring exhaustion of available administrative remedies.

issues.label: Exhaustion is claim-specific
issues.why: Each distinct claim must be exhausted through the prison’s process unless excused by unavailability.

issues.label: Available remedies question
issues.why: The court must determine whether VDOC remedies were actually “available” under Ross v. Blake.

issues.label: Unavailability: dead end
issues.why: If the process was a dead end (no possible relief), exhaustion may be excused.

issues.label: Unavailability: opaque process
issues.why: If grievance rules were so confusing that they were practically unusable, exhaustion may be excused.

issues.label: Unavailability: thwarting
issues.why: If officials interfered, intimidated, or misled Carter, remedies may be deemed unavailable.

issues.label: Proper exhaustion compliance
issues.why: The court must decide whether Carter complied with VDOC procedural requirements (timeliness, forms, levels, appeals).

issues.label: Intake rejection significance
issues.why: The court must determine whether a grievance rejected at intake can constitute exhaustion and what appeals were required.

issues.label: Effect of pending appeals
issues.why: The court must decide whether filing suit while intake appeals were pending fails exhaustion.

issues.label: Timing: suit commencement
issues.why: The key exhaustion moment is when the action is “brought,” requiring definition of commencement relative to original complaint.

issues.label: Amendment curing exhaustion
issues.why: The court must decide whether post-filing exhaustion plus an amended complaint can cure an initial failure to exhaust.

issues.label: Hardin v. Hunt applicability
issues.why: The court must determine whether the unpublished Hardin rule controls and how it fits with binding precedent.

issues.label: Relation-back implications
issues.why: If amended claims relate back under Rule 15(c), the court must consider how that affects exhaustion timing.

issues.label: New claims in amended complaint
issues.why: The court must decide whether First Amendment retaliation claims added later require exhaustion completed before the amendment or before the original filing.

issues.label: Separate exhaustion for retaliation
issues.why: The court must determine whether Carter exhausted the retaliation grievance as to each implicated actor and theory.

issues.label: Exhaustion for June complaint denial
issues.why: Because Carter never filed a regular grievance after the June informal complaint, the court must decide whether that issue was exhausted at all.

issues.label: Burden of proof exhaustion
issues.why: Exhaustion is an affirmative defense, so the court must allocate burdens and evaluate evidentiary showings.

issues.label: Summary judgment procedure
issues.why: The court must apply Rule 56 standards, including whether disputes of material fact on exhaustion exist.

issues.label: Need for discovery
issues.why: The court must consider whether granting summary judgment pre-discovery was proper or whether Rule 56(d) relief was warranted.

issues.label: Proper evidentiary materials
issues.why: The court must ensure grievances, policies, and declarations were admissible and properly authenticated at summary judgment.

issues.label: Notice to pro se litigant
issues.why: The court must ensure appropriate Roseboro-type notice and fair opportunity for Carter to respond to summary judgment.

issues.label: Choosing Rule 12 vs 56
issues.why: The court must use the correct procedural vehicle for exhaustion (often fact-intensive) and retaliation pleading sufficiency.

issues.label: Disposition form for nonexhaustion
issues.why: If nonexhaustion exists, the court must decide dismissal without prejudice versus with prejudice and proper judgment form.

issues.label: Partial exhaustion handling
issues.why: If some claims are exhausted and others are not, the court must decide severance/partial dismissal rather than wholesale dismissal.

issues.label: 1915A screening scope
issues.why: The court must ensure screening dismissal was limited to failure to state a claim and not premature factual determinations.

issues.label: Supervisory liability standard
issues.why: For Clarke, the court must apply correct §1983 supervisory-liability elements (knowledge, indifference, causation) under Fourth Circuit law.

issues.label: Policy/custom vs supervision
issues.why: The court must distinguish supervisory liability from liability for promulgating/enforcing unconstitutional policies or customs.

issues.label: Personal involvement requirement
issues.why: Each defendant must be linked to the constitutional violation through personal actions or omissions.

issues.label: Pleading sufficiency Clarke
issues.why: The court must decide whether allegations plausibly show Clarke knew of and disregarded a substantial risk to Carter specifically or via systemic notice.

issues.label: Reconsideration standard
issues.why: The court must apply the proper standard for reconsideration of the §1915A dismissal (Rule 54(b)/59(e)/60(b) as applicable).

issues.label: First Amendment protected activity
issues.why: The court must determine whether Carter’s informal complaint/grievances constitute protected speech/petitioning.

issues.label: Retaliation adverse action
issues.why: The court must decide whether denial of reentry/reclassification or continued RHU confinement would deter an ordinary person from protected activity.

issues.label: Retaliation causation
issues.why: The court must assess whether Carter plausibly/allegedly shows his protected activity was a motivating factor for the adverse action.

issues.label: Temporal proximity relevance
issues.why: The court must consider timing between complaints and adverse actions as circumstantial evidence of causation.

issues.label: Legitimate penological purpose
issues.why: The court must consider whether defendants had legitimate correctional reasons that defeat retaliation liability.

issues.label: Mt. Healthy burden shift
issues.why: The court must apply the burden-shifting framework: plaintiff motive showing then defendants’ same-decision defense.

issues.label: Retaliation by Branch
issues.why: The court must decide whether Branch’s alleged statements and conduct suffice to impose liability for retaliation.

issues.label: Retaliation by McCoy/Cabell
issues.why: The court must decide whether alleged references to wardens show their personal participation, direction, or tacit authorization.

issues.label: Bystander/acquiescence liability
issues.why: The court must consider whether non-speaking officials can be liable for retaliation via approval, direction, or failure to act.

issues.label: Qualified immunity retaliation
issues.why: The court must decide whether the right at issue was clearly established and whether reasonable officials could believe their conduct lawful.

issues.label: Eighth Amendment objective prong
issues.why: The court must determine whether RHU conditions posed a sufficiently serious deprivation of basic human needs or risk of serious harm.

issues.label: Eighth Amendment subjective prong
issues.why: The court must determine whether each defendant acted with deliberate indifference to a known substantial risk.

issues.label: Mental illness vulnerability
issues.why: Carter’s serious mental illnesses may affect the severity of harm and defendants’ awareness of risk.

issues.label: Porter v. Clarke comparison
issues.why: The court must evaluate whether Carter’s RHU conditions are materially similar to those held unconstitutional in Porter and over what time period.

issues.label: Duration and intensity of confinement
issues.why: The length and extremity of restrictive housing conditions are critical to the Eighth Amendment analysis.

issues.label: Conditions specifics needed
issues.why: The court must assess whether pleadings/evidence sufficiently specify isolation, out-of-cell time, human contact, programming, and sensory deprivation.

issues.label: Causation of injury
issues.why: For damages, Carter must show the conditions caused compensable physical or psychological injury.

issues.label: Physical injury requirement
issues.why: Under 42 U.S.C. §1997e(e), compensatory damages for mental/emotional injury may require prior physical injury, affecting available relief.

issues.label: Nominal and punitive damages
issues.why: Even if §1997e(e) limits compensatory damages, the court must consider availability of nominal and punitive damages for constitutional violations.

issues.label: PLRA limits on injunctions
issues.why: Any prospective relief must satisfy 18 U.S.C. §3626 requirements (narrowly drawn, least intrusive, necessary).

issues.label: Qualified immunity Eighth
issues.why: The court must decide whether clearly established law put officials on notice that the specific RHU conditions were unconstitutional.

issues.label: Liability of unnamed officials
issues.why: The court must address identification, service, amendment, and relation-back issues for John Doe defendants.

issues.label: Statute of limitations
issues.why: The court must ensure claims are timely under Virginia’s personal-injury limitations period and accrual rules for §1983.

issues.label: Continuing violation theory
issues.why: The court must decide whether ongoing confinement conditions permit a continuing-violation approach to timeliness and relief.

issues.label: PLRA filing fee/IFP rules
issues.why: The court must ensure compliance with PLRA fee requirements and potential three-strikes implications if relevant.

issues.label: Service of process adequacy
issues.why: The court must verify proper service on each defendant, especially given pro se and IFP status.

issues.label: Capacity pleadings clarity
issues.why: The court must determine whether defendants are sued in individual capacity, official capacity, or both, affecting immunity and remedies.

issues.label: Causation for supervisory defendants
issues.why: For any supervisory theory, the court must determine affirmative causal link between supervisor conduct/policy and Carter’s injury.

issues.label: Remedies against transferred inmate
issues.why: The court must determine what relief remains meaningful (damages vs declaratory/injunctive) after Carter’s transfer from Sussex.

issues.label: Declaratory relief mootness
issues.why: The court must assess whether declaratory relief is retrospective and thus improper or moot absent ongoing legal controversy.

issues.label: Standard of review on appeal
issues.why: To decide correctly, the court must apply the proper standards for §1915A dismissal, Rule 12(b)(6), and Rule 56 determinations.

issues.label: Harmless error assessment
issues.why: If procedural errors occurred (e.g., wrong standard), the court must decide whether they affected the outcome.
